description: Two-panel bright-field transmission electron micrograph pair of deformation substructures in polycrystalline Fe-16%Al (with less than 20 ppm C), both with a printed 0.2 µm scale bar in the lower-right corner and a dark vertical annotation strip (instrument/magnification text) along the right edge that is not legible. (a) Quenched from 1100 °C and deformed; (b) furnace cooled from 1100 °C and deformed; both were given 5.5% compressive strain at 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ at room temperature per the caption. Panel (a) shows several sets of intersecting glide bands (slip traces) running in various directions across the field, with predominantly straight, long, individual dislocations and only sparse local tangles between the bands. Panel (b), from the same alloy and strain but the furnace-cooled condition, shows a visibly denser and more tangled dislocation arrangement: dislocations lie in loose, wavy tangles and clusters between wider slip bands rather than as isolated straight lines. The two micrographs thus demonstrate that the quenched state leaves a lower-mobility, straight-dislocation/glide-band substructure, whereas furnace cooling permits more dislocation interaction and tangling at the same 5.5% compressive strain; no diffraction pattern, axis or numeric data are present in either panel.

observations.observation: Both panels are bright-field TEM micrographs of the same alloy family with an identical printed scale bar of 0.2 µm.
Panel (a) displays glide bands oriented in several different directions with mostly straight, long individual dislocations between the bands.
Panel (b) displays dislocations arranged as tangles and clustered groups between the glide bands, with a higher apparent dislocation density than (a).
Neither panel contains a diffraction pattern, axis, curve or printed numeric value other than the 0.2 µm scale bar.
A dark vertical strip of annotation text runs along the right edge of both micrographs; the characters are not legible at the supplied resolution.
The caption states the material is polycrystalline Fe-16%Al with less than 20 ppm C.
The caption states (a) is the quenched condition and (b) the furnace-cooled condition, both from 1100 °C.
The caption states both specimens received 5.5% compressive straining at a rate of 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ at room temperature.
The citing text states that glide bands in various directions with primarily straight dislocations between them were observed in the quenched Fe-16%Al alloy (Fig. 7(a)).
The citing text states that deformation of the furnace-cooled Fe-16%Al alloy led to dislocation tangles between the glide bands (Fig. 7(b)).
The citing text interprets these TEM observations as a reduced dislocation mobility for the higher Al content of 16% Al, enhanced by quenched-in excess vacancies.
The citing text contrasts this figure with Fig. 6 (Fe-12%Al with 60 ppm C), where cell formation occurred in the furnace-cooled alloy but not in the Fe-16%Al alloy.

subfigures.description: Bright-field TEM micrograph of quenched Fe-16%Al after 5.5% compressive strain, showing glide bands in various directions with primarily straight dislocations between them; 0.2 µm scale bar at lower right.

Bright-field TEM micrograph of the furnace-cooled Fe-16%Al alloy after the same 5.5% compressive strain, showing denser dislocation tangles clustered between the glide bands; 0.2 µm scale bar at lower right.
